extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical/Euclidean geometry; mathematicians studying Archimedean geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and proofs from Archimedes on conoids, spheroids, and the planar spiral: geometric propositions, lemmas, constructions, and the method-of-exhaustion style arguments used to compare areas and volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion via inscribed and circumscribed figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove equality (or inequalities) of curved solid volumes by inscribing and circumscribing sequences of simpler solids (cylinders, frusta, cones) whose differences can be made arbitrarily small; combine proportions of corresponding parts to arrive at contradiction if assumed inequality holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sequences of equal-axis cylinders/frusta inscribed in and circumscribed about the segment; compare sums via proportional relationships (use rectangles, gnomons, sums R_i) and Prop. 1–2 style results to force contradictions, concluding equality. Used repeatedly to compare spheroid segments with cones/segments of cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of a spheroid segment and a constructed cone V (segment ABB' = V)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a segment ABB' of a spheroid equals a particular cone or segment of cone V, assume inequality (segment > V or < V), inscribe/circumscribe equal cylinders/frusta to derive contradictions using proportional sums; conclude segment = V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed proof compares cylinder/frustum EB' with cone ABB' (ratio 3:1) and uses a proportional relation to V (via point H with CA' = A'H). The contradiction arises by selecting inscribed/circumscribed figures so that circumscribed−inscribed < (segment)−V, then deriving incompatible inequalities via sums of gnomons and rectangles (Prop. 1 & 2 style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special half-spheroid case: segment : cone = 2 : 1
rubrics_metrics.description: When the spheroid segment is exactly half the spheroid (CD or c/2 vanishes), the general rectangles simplify to squares and the ratio (segment ABB') : (cone or segment of cone ABB') equals 2 : 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by substituting CA for AD into the general ratio (86 — AD) : (2CA — AD) or by using the Lemma/Corollary to Prop. 2 (On Spirals, Prop. 10 lemma) to obtain the numerical ratio 3:2 for related quantities and hence 2:1 for segment:cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a plane divides spheroid into unequal segments, ratio to cone = CA+AN : AN
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane divides a spheroid into two unequal segments and AN, A'N are the axes of the lesser and greater segments while C is the centre, then (greater segment) : (cone or segment of cone with same base and axis) = CA+AN : AN.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct tangent-touch planes at A, A' and auxiliary cones whose vertices are A, A' and bases are the planar sections; use proportional equalities among cones and segments (and ex aequali arguments) together with geometric constructions producing points H,H' so AH = A'H' = CA, then combine ratios (using earlier propositions on halves etc.) to obtain the stated relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Archimedean spiral (Def. 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line drawn in a plane revolving uniformly about one fixed extremity while a point moves uniformly along the line from the fixed extremity describes a spiral (helix) in the plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the generating motion and uniform rates: one uniform angular motion and one uniform radial motion along the generating line; the spiral produced is the canonical 'Archimedean' spiral used in subsequent propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: origin of the spiral (Def. 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fixed extremity of the straight line about which the line revolves is called the origin of the spiral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for proofs and constructions that follow; many propositions refer to distances and arcs measured from this origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: initial line of the revolution (Def. 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial position of the straight line from which it began to revolve is called the initial line in the revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define arcs and orientations; used to define the 'first circle' etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: first/second/... distances and areas (Def. 4 & 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The length the moving point describes along the line in the first revolution is the first distance; the analogous lengths in later revolutions are subsequent distances. The area bounded by the spiral after the first revolution and the first distance is the first area; similarly define second area, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics let Archimedes relate spiral radii and areas to arcs and circle circumferences in proportional statements (e.g., Prop. 15, series-area relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: forward and backward directions (Def. 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the origin, any straight line drawn; the side in the direction of revolution is 'forward' and the opposite side is 'backward'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reason about whether radii vectores and comparison circles lie inside or outside the spiral (used in tangency/angle arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: first, second,... circles (Def. 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circle centered at origin with radius equal to the first distance is the first circle; twice that radius gives the second circle, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These circles provide reference circumferences (c) used in proportional formulae for distances and areas across revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1: lengths proportional to times under uniform motion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point moves uniformly along any line, two lengths taken on it are proportional to the times required to describe them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by equimultiples in Euclidean style (ref. Elements V. Def.5); basic kinematic proportionality used repeatedly to equate arc lengths and radial distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2: equal-time motion on different lines gives proportional lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: If two points move uniformly on different lines and pairs of lengths are described in equal times, those lengths are proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollary of Prop. 1; used to compare distances along different generating lines or arcs described on circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3: existence of straight line longer than sum of circumferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any finite set of circles, one can find a straight line greater than the sum of their circumferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction by circumscribing polygons and summing perimeters; used to ensure availability of arbitrarily large straight lengths for constructions in later propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4: intermediate straight line between given straight and circumference
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a straight line and a circle circumference, there exists a straight line less than the larger and greater than the smaller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the Lemma about repeated addition of excess to exceed any magnitude; constructive division of the straight line produces the desired intermediate length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5: construct OPF meeting circle and tangent so FP:OP < arc(AP):c
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a circle (center O) and its tangent at A and any circumference c, one can choose OPF meeting the circle in P and tangent in F such that FP:OP < (arc AP) : c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a straight line D greater than c and construct parallels so that PH equals D; use similar-triangle ratios FP:OP = AP:PH and compare to arc AP : c to get the inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6: construct OPF meeting chord AB and circle with given ratio FP:PB
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle center O, chord AB shorter than diameter and perpendicular OM, one can draw OPF meeting circle in P and chord in F so that FP:PB = D:E for any ratio D:E less than BM:MO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallels and similar triangles to relate OB:BT to BM:MO, choose PH so OB:PH = D:K and place PH to meet circle and OA line appropriately, then join OP and obtain required ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 7: construct OPF with FP:PB = D:E for ratio greater than BM:MO
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous construction as Prop.6 but for D:E greater than BM:MO; draw OT parallel to AB and proceed with circle-through points construction so that OP meets chord extension in F and yields FP:PB = D:E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetric method to Prop.6 using a different placement of auxiliary lines; both propositions show capability to realize arbitrary given ratios via geometric constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8: draw OPF meeting chord, circle and tangent so FP:BG = D:E (D:E less than BM:MO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle, chord AB, tangent at B and perpendicular OM, can draw OFP meeting chord AB in F, circle in P and tangent in G such that FP:BG = D:E for D:E less than BM:MO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct auxiliary point C' on tangent, draw circle through O, 7', C, pick GQ equal to KB, build triangle relations and use proportional equalities OP:OF = BC:CG to derive FP:BG = D:E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9: analogue for D:E greater than BM:MO with AB produced
rubrics_metrics.description: Same type as Prop.8 but for target ratio greater than BM:MO; construct circle through O,7,C and line OGQ meeting circle and tangent to obtain PF:BG = D:E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows same pattern as Prop.8 with reversed inequalities and placement so that AB is produced; demonstrates flexibility of constructions to achieve desired segment-to-tangent ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10: sum of squares formula for arithmetic progression terms
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1, A2,...,An form an ascending arithmetic progression with common difference equal to A1, then (n+1)A1^2 + A1(A1 + A2 + ... + An) = 3(A1^2 + A2^2 + ... + An^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical summation identity shown earlier (relates to n(n+1)(2n+1)/6); corollaries give inequalities bounding sums of squares and linear sums; remark that similar figures can replace squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11: inequalities for sums of squares in arithmetic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: For A1,...,An in ascending arithmetic progression with common difference equal to A1, two inequalities relate (n−1)A1^2 to sums of squares and mixed terms; corollaries allow substitution of similar figures for squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long constructive/schematic proof using side-by-side arrangement of terms; results provide technical inequalities used in bounding sums in later exhaustion arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (stated earlier): excess can be multiplied to exceed any given comparable magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal lines or areas, the excess by which the greater exceeds the less can, by being continually added to itself, be made to exceed any given magnitude comparable with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to produce integers n such that n·(excess) exceeds some target; underlies constructions in Propositions 3–5 and the method-of-exhaustion arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 12: radial lines at equal angles form arithmetic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: If any number of straight lines drawn from origin to meet the spiral make equal angles with one another, the lengths of those lines (radii) are in arithmetic progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from the uniform angular and linear motion definition of the spiral; used to connect equal angular partitioning to arithmetic radial steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 13: a tangent to the spiral touches in exactly one point
rubrics_metrics.description: Any straight line tangent to the spiral meets it at a single point only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume two contact points, bisect angle between their radii to get an intermediate radius violating triangle bisector inequality, forcing the tangent to cut the spiral — contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 14: ratio of radii equals ratio of corresponding arcs on first circle
rubrics_metrics.description: For points P,Q on first turn, with OP and OQ produced to meet first circle in P',Q', OP:OQ = (arc AKP') : (arc AKQ').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While generating point moves uniformly on OA, corresponding point A on circle moves uniformly along arc; apply Prop.2 (equal-time proportionality) to equate distances to arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15: radii on second turn relate to circumference + arc
rubrics_metrics.description: If P,Q on second turn, OP:OQ = c + (arc AKP') : c + (arc AKQ'), where c is circumference of first circle; generalization: on nth turn use (n−1)c + arc terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the fact that the moving point on OA experiences full circumferences plus arcs while the generating point completes revolutions; shows how global circumference enters proportional relations for later turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 16–17: tangent angle relations (OPC obtuse, OPB acute)
rubrics_metrics.description: For tangent BC at point P on spiral, letting PC be the 'forward' part, join OP: the angle OPC is obtuse while OPB (backward side) is acute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument compares the spiral to circle of radius OP and uses Prop.5 style constructions and inequalities involving arcs; extends to points on any nth turn by adding multiples of circumference to arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions 18–19: perpendicular from origin meets tangent at point whose distance equals circle circumference multiples
rubrics_metrics.description: If OA is initial line and A is end of first turn, straight line OB drawn from O perpendicular to OA meets tangent at A in B with OB equal to circumference of first circle; for A' (end of second turn), OB' equals 2·(circumference), and generally OB_n = n·(circumference of nth circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses contradiction by assuming OB > c or OB < c, then constructing auxiliary points (e.g., F, P, Q) and using Propositions 5/15 to derive impossible inequalities; shows deep connection between tangent geometry and circumference lengths.
